blockingFindings.detail: GREEN evidence can be forged by normal malicious artifact input, with no race needed. The verdict rests only on the runner's process exit code. That process executes model-authored code. An allowed source file containing top-level `import os; os._exit(0)` makes the oracle process exit 0 as soon as the test imports the module. The result is red!=0 at base, green==0 at the result commit, scope clean and oracle bytes intact, so status becomes 'verified' even though no oracle assertion ran. The same class of forgery works if the code patches unittest/pytest reporting in-process, or edits an oracle or tracked file during GREEN and restores it before exit (post-run hash and clean checks only see the final state). `_is_test_path` segregation is also a name heuristic. allowedFiles may include `pyproject.toml`, `pytest.ini`, `setup.cfg`, `tox.ini`, `sitecustomize.py`/`usercustomize.py`, or package `__init__.py` files outside tests/. Through these the model can reconfigure or neutralize the oracle, e.g. `addopts = --collect-only` exits 0. This contradicts the module and handoff claim that a completed result requires host-observed evidence. Minimum fix before merge: (a) do not label exit==0 as 'verified'. Require a trusted, out-of-band report from the runner (expected oracle test IDs/count all executed and passed, written outside the model-writable tree, bound to a per-run nonce) and extend the runner contract to return it. Or rename the status to make clear it is untrusted-exit-code evidence. (b) Reject interpreter/test-framework config and import-hook files from allowedFiles, or require explicit reviewed opt-in. (c) Add a regression test showing that an `os._exit(0)` artifact is not 'verified'.

The public entry does not validate its contract. `execute_approved` never calls `load_contract`, and `parse_result_envelope` applies only exact membership in `contract['allowedFiles']`, never `check_path`, to model paths. Every path, test-segregation, oracle-disjointness, limits and baseSha guarantee therefore depends on each caller having pre-validated the dict. The approval digest does not help: it is computed by the same code over whatever dict is passed. Concrete consequences with an unvalidated contract such as `allowedFiles: ['../escape.py']`: `_checked_path` walks `root/..` (a real directory, so lstat passes) and `materialize` writes and `os.replace`s `dest/../escape.py` outside the copy. The post-write re-check passes. Only the later `git add` fails, after the out-of-copy write has persisted. The same gap allows `.git/config` or `.git/...` targets (the fresh repo's local config then controls later git invocations beyond the -c overrides) and test paths in allowedFiles. Fix: `execute_approved` must run `load_contract` itself and use its returned canonical copy for the digest and all later steps. `parse_result_envelope` should also run `check_path` on each model path as defense in depth. Add a test that passes a raw, unvalidated contract dict to `execute_approved`.

followups.detail: The previous blocker was that two concurrent whole-state saves in one useDesktopState could roll back to an old state while keeping the newer revision, after which the next save passed CAS and erased data. Within one panel instance this is fixed. saveLockRef is checked and set synchronously before mutate() is called. It is released only in a useLayoutEffect keyed on settledCount. setSettledCount is queued after mutate's post-await setState/setRevision calls in the same lane, so the committed render that runs the effect already contains the settled state and revision. Any event that arrives between the settle and the React render hits the held lock and is dropped. No second mutate can capture a stale previous/previousRevision. Every mutating path goes through run(): add/toggle/remove criterion and step, advance, goToEarlierPhase, editSetting, removeSetting, addRule, removeRule, addDecision, togglePin. Because of this, a failure rollback restores the last server-confirmed state, so state and revision stay consistent and a later conflict shows up as a visible 409. blockingFindings.detail: GREEN evidence can be forged by normal malicious artifact input, with no race needed. The verdict rests only on the runner's process exit code. That process executes model-authored code. An allowed source file containing top-level `import os; os._exit(0)` makes the oracle process exit 0 as soon as the test imports the module. The result is red!=0 at base, green==0 at the result commit, scope clean and oracle bytes intact, so status becomes 'verified' even though no oracle assertion ran. The same class of forgery works if the code patches unittest/pytest reporting in-process, or edits an oracle or tracked file during GREEN and restores it before exit (post-run hash and clean checks only see the final state). `_is_test_path` segregation is also a name heuristic. allowedFiles may include `pyproject.toml`, `pytest.ini`, `setup.cfg`, `tox.ini`, `sitecustomize.py`/`usercustomize.py`, or package `__init__.py` files outside tests/. Through these the model can reconfigure or neutralize the oracle, e.g. `addopts = --collect-only` exits 0. This contradicts the module and handoff claim that a completed result requires host-observed evidence. Minimum fix before merge: (a) do not label exit==0 as 'verified'. Require a trusted, out-of-band report from the runner (expected oracle test IDs/count all executed and passed, written outside the model-writable tree, bound to a per-run nonce) and extend the runner contract to return it. Or rename the status to make clear it is untrusted-exit-code evidence. (b) Reject interpreter/test-framework config and import-hook files from allowedFiles, or require explicit reviewed opt-in. (c) Add a regression test showing that an `os._exit(0)` artifact is not 'verified'.

The public entry does not validate its contract. `execute_approved` never calls `load_contract`, and `parse_result_envelope` applies only exact membership in `contract['allowedFiles']`, never `check_path`, to model paths. blockingFindings.detail: The pass verdict does not verify that capture and exit actually completed, so it can fail open. (1) After a normal proc.wait(), each pump thread gets thread.join(timeout=5), but is_alive() is never checked. A lagging pump yields a truncated stdout snapshot, and the code still compares and hashes it (a prefix can equal expectedStdout). (2) proc.returncode, the docker start -a client exit code, is never read or cross-checked against State.ExitCode. (3) The inspected State is never checked for Status=='exited', Running==false, or a non-empty Error. A still-running container reports ExitCode 0. Together these mean that if the attach stream is lost or the client exits abnormally while the container keeps running, passed=True is reachable with ExitCode 0 plus partial stdout. Under normal Docker semantics, start -a waits for container exit, so hostile code cannot trigger this directly. It is an infrastructure-anomaly path, but the oracle's only job is a trustworthy verdict. Fix: treat any pump or feed thread that is still alive as a failure; require proc.returncode == State.ExitCode; require Status=='exited', Running false, and an empty Error; otherwise raise OracleError or mark the case failed. Add tests that mock a live pump and a Running state.

blockingFindings.detail: The pass verdict does not verify that capture and exit actually completed, so it can fail open. (1) After a normal proc.wait(), each pump thread gets thread.join(timeout=5), but is_alive() is never checked. A lagging pump yields a truncated stdout snapshot, and the code still compares and hashes it (a prefix can equal expectedStdout). (2) proc.returncode, the docker start -a client exit code, is never read or cross-checked against State.ExitCode. (3) The inspected State is never checked for Status=='exited', Running==false, or a non-empty Error. A still-running container reports ExitCode 0. Together these mean that if the attach stream is lost or the client exits abnormally while the container keeps running, passed=True is reachable with ExitCode 0 plus partial stdout. Under normal Docker semantics, start -a waits for container exit, so hostile code cannot trigger this directly. It is an infrastructure-anomaly path, but the oracle's only job is a trustworthy verdict. Fix: treat any pump or feed thread that is still alive as a failure; require proc.returncode == State.ExitCode; require Status=='exited', Running false, and an empty Error; otherwise raise OracleError or mark the case failed. Add tests that mock a live pump and a Running state.

Pre-wiring gate. Only the contract is revalidated. The copy, materialized, red and source_before handles are trusted caller state. (a) A forged copy['root'] or rootIdentity lets materialize write allowed files under any root, including sourceRepo; separation from sourceRepo is only checked in create_task_copy. (b) A copy is not bound to its contract: copy['oracle'] can come from a different contract than the one passed in. (c) materialized['resultCommit'] and copy['baseCommit'] reach `git diff-tree` in _changed with no hex40 check and no --end-of-options. A value like `--output=<path>` would be option injection if these handles are ever deserialized from the store or routes. (d) Forged red or source_before make exitPatternObserved and sourceWorktreeBytesUnchanged caller-asserted. This is harmless now, because verification is always blocked and the handles are in-process. Before wiring: keep them in-process only, or bind them to contract_digest and validate hex40 plus root separation. Also document these handles as caller-asserted, not validated.

The docstring says 'every public entry re-validates the contract itself'. That is overbroad for the two digest helpers; the handoff discloses the gap. Related: load_contract does not reject strings that cannot be encoded as UTF-8 (lone surrogates) in sourceRepo, argv, task or model. The digest encode then raises a raw UnicodeEncodeError instead of ArtifactError. This still fails closed and happens before any side effect.

_require_separate_dest accepts a dest with missing parents, but os.mkdir is non-recursive. An existing dest therefore surfaces raw FileNotFoundError or FileExistsError instead of ArtifactError. _root_identity also refuses a dest whose ancestors are spelled with 8.3 or divergent case, because resolve() differs from absolute(). This can happen when %TEMP% uses a short name. Both fail closed. Normalize the error type and document the spelling requirement.

followups: CRITICAL PRE-WIRING GATE (residual fail-open, not introduced by 8440f6c): pump completion is inferred negatively. `failed` is set only for (OSError, ValueError). Any other exception in a pump (e.g. MemoryError or an unexpected stream type) kills the thread without setting `failed` and without killing the client. After join the thread is no longer alive, so a truncated stdout prefix can still reach the comparison. This path exists because the t3 fix was narrowed from `except Exception` to satisfy ruff BLE001, and no RED ever covered non-OSError exceptions. Fix: have each pump set a per-stream `completed` event only on EOF (b"") or overflow, and require both before any verdict. The feed thread should likewise record whether the full stdin was delivered; today a mid-write OSError on a still-live pipe is swallowed, so a verdict can be computed over truncated input.

`_attach` closes proc.stdin after the threads finish. If feed's write raised BrokenPipe with bytes still buffered, which happens when a program exits without draining a large stdin, `stdin.close()` re-flushes and raises a raw OSError. That is fail-closed, not a wrong PASS, but it is a spurious untyped failure for legitimate programs. Suppress OSError on the stdin close, as Popen.communicate does. Add a test: a program that ignores 64 KiB of stdin and exits 0 with correct output must pass.
